slides.say: A and B represent nonzero digits. Which of the following necessarily divides A B plus B A?

We add a two-digit number to the number with its digits reversed. We need a divisor that always works for their sum. There is no given result to check column by column. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, trying numbers, and then writing the numbers using their place values.

[short pause] Let's start by plugging in digits. Use A is seven and B is one. A B is seventy-one, and B A is seventeen. Seventy-one plus seventeen is eighty-eight. Eighty-eight is not divisible by three or ten, so choice numbers two and three are out.

Two choices remain. Try a different pair of digits: seventy-two plus twenty-seven is ninety-nine. Ninety-nine is not divisible by four, so that choice is out. Only eleven remains. Choice number one is our answer.
at: choice number one is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's write the number using its digits to see why eleven always works. In A B, A is the tens digit and B is the ones digit. So A B means ten times A plus B. For example, forty-seven is ten times four plus seven.

For a three-digit number A B C, A is the hundreds digit, B is the tens digit, and C is the ones digit. Its value is a hundred times A, plus ten times B, plus C. Five hundred thirty-eight is five hundred plus thirty plus eight.

Write both numbers that way. A B plus B A is ten A plus B, plus ten B plus A. Add the A parts to get eleven A, and the B parts to get eleven B. That is eleven times the whole bracket, A plus B. So the sum is always divisible by eleven. Choice number one is our answer.
at: ten A plus B, plus ten B

slides.say: For subtraction, use the same idea. A B minus B A is nine times the whole bracket, A minus B. Sixty-two minus twenty-six is thirty-six, which is four times nine. Both patterns appear in exam questions. Writing the place values explains the rule; testing two numbers can also rule out the other choices quickly. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
